profiles.name: Martin Carter
profiles.description: Martin Carter was executed with Starling Clayton in Barnwell District, South Carolina, for assisting fugitive slaves. The case is recorded in the Espy chronology under “Aid Runaway Slave,” and legal-history references identify State v. Clayton and Carter as an 1858 South Carolina prosecution for assisting fugitives. Later execution chronologies give February 25, 1859, as the hanging date. The surviving summaries do not identify the people they helped or establish Carter’s organizational ties.

profiles.name: William Smith
profiles.description: William Smith was a Black seaman executed in Chatham County, Georgia, on September 8, 1810. The Espy execution chronology classifies his offense as aiding a runaway slave; Georgia execution records describe the prosecution as slave stealing involving an enslaved woman and her child. The surviving summary does not preserve their names, the circumstances of their attempted escape, or Smith’s stated motive. It does establish that Georgia used capital punishment against a Black seaman accused of helping remove two people from slavery.
profiles.finding: Geologist, actor, priest and later soldier namesakes excluded from Black seaman executed1810.

profiles.name: John Black
profiles.description: John Black was among a group of white men hanged in Gadsden County, Florida, in 1846. The Espy chronology classifies Black, Alvin Flowers, and Thomas Smith under “Aid Runaway Slave” and dates their executions to October 2. Other later execution compilations place the same group in a mail-robbery and murder prosecution and disagree about the date. Because the surviving summaries conflict and do not separate each man’s conduct, Black’s profile records the Espy classification while leaving his precise role and motive unresolved.
profiles.finding: Senator portrait and genealogical John Black records not matched to1846 execution.
profiles.rights: No image accepted; public accessibility does not establish public-domain status

profiles.name: Alanson Work
profiles.description: Alanson Work was a carpenter and committed abolitionist associated with the Mission Institute at Quincy, Illinois. On July 13, 1841, he crossed into Marion County, Missouri, with James E. Burr and George Thompson to help enslaved people escape across the Mississippi River. The intended passengers disclosed the plan, and the three men were seized, threatened by a mob, convicted of larceny described as slave abduction, and sentenced to twelve years of hard labor. Governor John C. Edwards pardoned Work on January 20, 1845, after three years, six months, and seven days, on the condition that he take his family back to Connecticut.
profiles.finding: Dickinson Underground Railroad handbook identifies subject; no standalone portrait verified.

profiles.name: James E. Burr
profiles.description: James E. Burr was an abolitionist ministry student at the Mission Institute in Quincy, Illinois. He joined Alanson Work and George Thompson in crossing the Mississippi River on July 13, 1841, to help enslaved Missourians escape to Illinois and onward to Canada. The plan was betrayed, and all three were captured, convicted of larceny or slave abduction, and sentenced to twelve years of hard labor. Burr remained imprisoned for a little more than four and a half years before receiving a pardon in January 1846.

profiles.name: George Thompson
profiles.description: George Thompson was a New Jersey-born abolitionist and ministry student at the Mission Institute in Quincy, Illinois. On July 13, 1841, he crossed into Marion County, Missouri, with Alanson Work and James E. Burr to help enslaved people escape to Canada. Their plan was disclosed and the three were captured, convicted of larceny described as slave abduction, and sentenced to twelve years of hard labor. Thompson served the longest of the three, nearly five years, until Governor John C. Edwards pardoned him on June 24, 1846. He wrote the group’s prison narrative and later became a Congregational minister and missionary.

profiles.name: Elijah Anderson
profiles.description: Elijah Anderson was a free Black blacksmith and one of the Underground Railroad’s most active conductors along the Ohio River. He claimed to have helped roughly eight hundred people reach freedom while working from Madison, Indiana, and another thousand from Lawrenceburg. Kentucky officers arrested him aboard the steamboat Superior on December 17, 1856. After an initial acquittal, authorities immediately rearrested him, held and tortured him for months while demanding the names of collaborators, and convicted him of helping an enslaved man named George escape. Anderson received eight years and eight months in the Kentucky State Penitentiary. He was found dead in his cell on March 4, 1861, the day one account says he was due to be released.

profiles.name: Charles Doy
profiles.description: Charles Doy was the nineteen-year-old son of Underground Railroad conductor John Doy. He accompanied his father and thirteen Black passengers on a January 1859 journey from Lawrence, Kansas Territory, toward Nebraska. Armed Missourians seized the party on January 25 and carried John and Charles across the state line, where both were committed to jail on allegations of abducting enslaved people. Charles remained imprisoned at Platte City until the first trial at St. Joseph on March 20, when prosecutors abandoned the case against him and released him. He later joined the Kansas party that returned to St. Joseph and rescued his father from jail.

profiles.name: Christopher Solomon Proctor
profiles.description: Christopher Solomon Proctor is a Salt Lake City man and self-described anarchist held in federal pretrial detention over an alleged September 12, 2025 attempt to burn a KSTU-TV news vehicle. Prosecutors allege that a masked person placed a gasoline can with a long fuse beneath the parked vehicle and lit it; the fuse burned out before reaching the gasoline, and nobody was injured. Investigators say DNA on the can matched Proctor, surveillance and license-plate-reader records placed him near the station, and searches recovered similar boots, gloves, a gas can, and fuse. Proctor was arrested on September 29, indicted the following day for attempted arson affecting interstate commerce and possession of an unregistered destructive device, and pleaded not guilty. On October 6, Magistrate Judge Dustin Pead ordered him detained pending trial. The allegations remain unproved, and the latest public reporting located for this profile did not establish a conviction, release, or final disposition.
profiles.finding: Salt Lake Tribune and AP case coverage; no verified face portrait inspected.
